analysis.one_liner: Bars employers from canceling workers' health insurance while locking them out in a labor dispute.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee in July 2022 and died there when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: When a company locks out employees to pressure their union before a strike, the lockout cuts off pay and, under current law, can also cut off the employer-provided health insurance that workers and their families depend on. This bill would make it an unfair labor practice for an employer to terminate or change a locked-out employee's health coverage during the lockout, with civil penalties of up to $75,000 per violation — doubled to $150,000 for repeat offenders, and with possible personal liability for company directors and officers who direct the violation.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who are locked out by their employers during collective bargaining, and their families, who would keep their health insurance through the lockout instead of losing coverage and having to pay out of pocket for care or buy expensive replacement insurance.

how_it_helps.text: Adds a new unfair labor practice to the National Labor Relations Act: an employer may not terminate or alter an employee's group health plan coverage during a lockout, suspension, or other withholding of employment used to influence collective bargaining. [S3]

Attaches civil penalties up to $75,000 per violation, doubled to $150,000 when the violation coincides with a discharge or causes serious economic harm and the employer violated the same rule within the previous five years. [S3]

Allows the labor board to assess penalties personally against a director or officer who directed the violation, knew of it and could have prevented it, or had authority to prevent it and failed to. [S3]
Requires the board to weigh the gravity of the employer's conduct, the impact on workers, the employer's size, its history of violations, and the public interest when setting penalties. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Employers that use lockouts as a negotiating tactic would lose the ability to cut off health coverage as leverage, would face civil penalties up to $75,000 per violation (up to $150,000 for repeat violations), and could face personal penalties on their executives. Employers that do not lock out workers would be unaffected.

drawbacks.text: Lockouts are a legal negotiating tool, and the bill would raise the cost of using one: an employer could no longer withdraw the health benefit it provides, which some employers argue is a legitimate part of economic pressure in bargaining. [S3]
The bill is narrow: it protects only health coverage during lockouts and leaves other pressures on locked-out workers, including lost wages, unchanged. [S3]
Penalties of up to $75,000 per violation, even doubled, are small for large employers and may not deter a determined company. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete for a specific, vulnerable group: locked-out workers would not have to fear losing their family's health insurance as a bargaining tactic. The cost falls on a small set of employers that use lockouts, and the penalty amounts are modest by corporate standards. The main weakness is narrowness — it does nothing about wages lost during a lockout — but within its scope the protection is straightforward and enforceable.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing or voted on it, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Axne introduced the bill with six Democratic cosponsors on July 13, 2022. [S1]
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor. [S5]
No further action was ever taken on the bill: no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote. [S5]
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill expired with it. [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that use lockouts to pressure unions keep the ability to cut off workers' health coverage during a lockout, with no new penalty attached. Locked-out workers gain nothing; the bill never advanced far enough for anyone to vote on it.

industries.industry: Employers that use lockouts in labor disputes
industries.note: The bill removes one of their bargaining levers — cutting off employees' health coverage during a lockout — and adds civil penalties up to $75,000 per violation, doubled to $150,000 for repeat violations, with possible personal liability for executives. Workers locked out by such employers would keep their insurance.

industries.industry: Employer group health plans and insurers
industries.note: Coverage that would otherwise be terminated mid-lockout would stay in place, keeping premiums flowing on plans workers and their families depend on. The effect is modest.
